1.28.oldText: BARNARDO. Sit down for a moment, and let us try once more to convince you — you who are so resistant to our story — of what we've seen these past two nights.

1.48.oldText: HORATIO. As much as you look like yourself. That was the very armor he wore when he fought the ambitious King of Norway, and that was the same frown he had when, in an angry confrontation, he struck down the Polish forces on the ice. It's strange.

1.52.oldText: HORATIO. I can — at least, the rumor goes like this. Our late King, whose image just appeared to us, was challenged to single combat by Fortinbras of Norway, who was driven by fierce competitive pride. Our brave King Hamlet — as the whole world honored him — killed this Fortinbras, who, by a legally sealed agreement, forfeited all the lands he possessed to the conqueror. In return, our King had wagered an equal portion of his own lands, which would have gone to Fortinbras had he won — as the terms of the same contract specified. Now, young Fortinbras — full of untested ambition and hot blood — has been gathering up a ragtag army of lawless mercenaries from the fringes of Norway, feeding them for some bold enterprise. And that enterprise, as our state well knows, is nothing less than taking back by force the lands his father lost. That, I believe, is the main reason for our preparations, the source of this watch, and the chief cause of all the frantic activity in the land.

1.53.oldText: BARNARDO. I think you're right. It makes sense that this ominous figure would come marching through our watch in armor, looking like the King who was at the center of these wars.

1.54.oldText: HORATIO. It's a speck that troubles the mind's eye. In Rome at its height, just before the mighty Julius Caesar fell, the graves stood empty and the shrouded dead walked shrieking through the streets. There were stars with trails of fire, bloody dew, disasters in the sun, and the moon — which governs the tides — was eclipsed almost to the point of doomsday. And similar omens, like heralds announcing what fate has in store, have been shown by heaven and earth together to our own land and people.

1.56.oldText: HORATIO. But wait — look! There it comes again! I'll cross its path, even if it destroys me. Stop, illusion! If you can make any sound or use your voice, speak to me. If there is any good deed that can be done to give you peace and me grace, speak to me. If you know something about our country's fate that, if known in advance, we might prevent — speak! Or if in life you buried stolen treasure in the ground, for which they say spirits often walk after death — tell us about it. Stop and speak!

1.59.oldText: MARCELLUS. Should I strike it with my weapon?

1.64.oldText: MARCELLUS. It's gone! We were wrong to threaten it — it's so majestic. We were foolish to show it violence. It's as untouchable as the air, and our blows were nothing but mockery.

1.66.oldText: HORATIO. And then it flinched, like a guilty person caught in the act. I've heard that the rooster, which is the trumpet call of morning, wakes the god of day with its loud, clear call, and at that warning, every wandering spirit — whether in sea, fire, earth, or air — hurries back to its place of confinement. And what we just saw proves it.

1.68.oldText: HORATIO. I've heard that too, and I partly believe it. But look — the morning, dressed in reddish brown, is walking over the dew on that hill to the east. Let's end our watch, and I suggest we tell young Hamlet what we've seen tonight. I'm certain this spirit, which was silent with us, will speak to him. Do you agree we should let him know? It's our duty, and our love demands it.

2.3.oldText: KING. Though the memory of our dear brother Hamlet's death is still fresh, and it was right for us to grieve with heavy hearts, and for the whole kingdom to wear a look of sorrow — still, wisdom has fought with natural feeling, and we've decided to mourn him with sensible grief while also thinking of ourselves. Therefore, our former sister-in-law, now our queen and co-ruler of this warlike state, we have married — with a kind of defeated joy, one eye weeping and the other smiling, with mirth at the funeral and mourning at the wedding, balancing happiness and sorrow equally. We have not ignored your wise counsel, which has freely supported this decision. We thank you all. Now, you should know that young Fortinbras, thinking little of our strength, or believing our late brother's death has left our state weak and disorganized, has pestered us with messages demanding the surrender of lands his father legally lost to our most valiant brother. So much for him. Now, for ourselves and for this meeting: we have written to the King of Norway, uncle to young Fortinbras — who is old, bedridden, and barely aware of his nephew's plans — asking him to put a stop to this, since the troops being raised come from Norwegian subjects. We send you, good Cornelius, and you, Voltemand, as bearers of this message to old Norway, giving you no authority beyond what these detailed documents allow. Farewell, and let your speed show your loyalty. CORNELIUS and VOLTEMAND. In that and all things, we will show our duty.

2.14.oldText: QUEEN. Dear Hamlet, put off this dark mood, and look on the King of Denmark as a friend. Don't keep looking down with lowered eyes, searching for your noble father in the dust. You know it's the way of things — everything that lives must die, passing through nature into eternity.

2.18.oldText: KING. It's sweet and honorable of you, Hamlet, to pay these mourning duties to your father. But you must know that your father lost a father, and that father lost his, and each surviving son was bound by duty to grieve for a time. But to keep on with this stubborn mourning is a show of defiance toward heaven. It's unmanly grief; it reveals a weak heart, an impatient mind, and a simple understanding. Since what must be is as common as anything we experience, why should we stubbornly resist it? It's a fault against heaven, a fault against the dead, a fault against nature, and completely absurd — since the most universal truth is that fathers die, and every generation from the first has cried, 'This must be so.' We ask you to put aside this useless grief and think of us as a father. Let the world know: you are next in line for our throne, and we care for you with no less love than a devoted father has for his son. As for your plan to go back to school in Wittenberg, that's the opposite of what we want. We ask you to stay here in the comfort and warmth of our presence — our chief courtier, our nephew, and our son.

2.21.oldText: KING. That's a loving and proper answer. Consider yourself at home here in Denmark. Madam, come — this gentle and willing agreement from Hamlet warms my heart. In honor of it, every toast the King of Denmark drinks today shall be announced with cannon fire, and the heavens themselves shall echo the thunder. Come, let's go.

2.23.oldText: HAMLET. Oh, if only this too-solid body would just melt, dissolve, and turn into dew! Or if God hadn't forbidden suicide. Oh God! Oh God! How exhausting, stale, flat, and pointless everything in this world seems to me! What a disgusting place — like a garden no one tends, overrun with weeds. Things rank and gross in nature have completely taken over. That it should come to this! Dead only two months — no, not even two. Such an excellent king, who was to this one as a sun god is to a goat. So loving to my mother that he wouldn't let the wind blow too roughly on her face. Heaven and earth — do I have to remember? She would hang on him as if her appetite grew by feeding on him. And yet, within a month — don't let me think about it. Frailty, thy name is woman! A mere month — before the shoes were even old that she wore following my poor father's coffin, crying like Niobe. And she — even she — oh God! A mindless animal would have mourned longer — married my uncle, my father's brother, who is no more like my father than I am like Hercules. Within a month — before the salt of her shameful tears had even dried in her reddened eyes — she married. Oh, what wicked haste, to rush so eagerly to an incestuous bed! This is not good, and it cannot lead to anything good. But break, my heart — I must keep silent.

2.26.oldText: HAMLET. I'm glad to see you well — Horatio, unless I'm mistaken.

2.32.oldText: HAMLET. I wouldn't let your enemy say that about you, and I won't let you say it either. I know you're no truant. But what's your business in Elsinore? We'll teach you to drink heavily before you leave.

2.47.oldText: HORATIO. Two nights in a row, these gentlemen — Marcellus and Barnardo — while on their watch in the dead of night, had this encounter. A figure exactly like your father, fully armed from head to toe, appeared before them and walked slowly and majestically past them three times, staying within the length of a staff, while they — practically turned to jelly with fear — stood dumb and speechless. They told me about this in the strictest secrecy. I kept watch with them the third night, and exactly as they had described — the same time, the same form, every detail proven true — the ghost appeared. I knew your father. These two hands look no more alike.

2.67.oldText: HORATIO. It would have amazed you.

2.71.oldText: HAMLET. His beard was grey, wasn't it?

2.79.oldText: HAMLET. My father's ghost, in armor! Something is very wrong. I suspect foul play. I wish night would come! Until then, be still, my soul. Foul deeds will rise to the surface, no matter how deeply they're buried.

3.3.oldText: LAERTES. As for Hamlet and his attention to you — treat it as nothing more than a passing fancy, a youthful impulse. Think of it as a violet in spring — beautiful but not lasting. Sweet, but only for a moment. Nothing more.

3.5.oldText: LAERTES. Don't think of it as more. A young man doesn't just grow physically — as the body develops, so do the mind and soul. Perhaps he loves you now, and right now no dishonesty taints his intentions. But you have to understand — given his position, his will is not his own. He's bound by his birth. He can't just choose for himself the way ordinary people do, because the health and security of the whole state depends on his choices. So when he says he loves you, you'd be wise to believe it only as far as someone in his position can actually follow through — and that goes no further than what Denmark itself allows. Think about what you could lose if you listen too eagerly to his sweet talk, or give your heart away, or surrender your chastity to his reckless pursuit. Be careful, Ophelia — my dear sister. Stay back, out of the firing range of desire. Even the most careful young woman risks too much if she reveals her beauty to the world. Virtue itself can't escape vicious gossip. The worm destroys the bud in spring before it even opens, and in the fresh dew of youth, disease is most dangerous. Be cautious — safety lies in being careful. Youth rebels against itself, even without outside temptation.

3.6.oldText: OPHELIA. I'll take this good advice to heart. But dear brother, don't be like those hypocritical preachers who show me the steep and thorny road to heaven while they themselves walk the easy path of pleasure, ignoring their own advice.

3.9.oldText: LAERTES. A second farewell is a double blessing — fortune smiles on a second leave-taking.

3.12.oldText: POLONIUS. And remember these few rules. Keep your thoughts to yourself, and don't act on any rash impulse. Be friendly, but not common. Hold tight to the friends you've tested and found true — bind them to your soul with hoops of steel. But don't waste your time on every new acquaintance you meet. Stay out of fights, but if you're in one, make sure your opponent fears you. Listen to everyone, but confide in few. Consider everyone's opinion, but reserve your own judgment. Dress as well as you can afford, but don't be flashy — expensive, not gaudy. Clothes often reveal the man, and in France, the best people dress with taste and distinction. Neither borrow nor lend money — lending often loses both the money and the friend, and borrowing dulls the edge of good management. Above all: be true to yourself. And it must follow, as night follows day, that you cannot then be false to anyone. Farewell — may my blessing make this wisdom take root in you.

3.21.oldText: POLONIUS. Well remembered. I've been told that he's been spending a lot of private time with you lately, and that you've been very generous in granting him your company. If that's true — and I've been warned about it as a matter of concern — I have to tell you that you don't understand yourself as clearly as a daughter of mine should. What's going on between you? Tell me the truth.

3.27.oldText: POLONIUS. Honorable? Ha! That's one word for it.

3.29.oldText: POLONIUS. Those are just traps to catch the unwary. I know that when the blood runs hot, the soul recklessly makes promises. These flashes, daughter — giving more light than heat, burning out even as they're being made — you must not mistake for genuine fire. From now on, be less available. Set a higher price on your time than to come running whenever he asks. As for Lord Hamlet, believe this much about him: he is young, and he has a longer leash than you do. In short, Ophelia, don't believe his promises. They're go-betweens — not what they appear to be — mere promoters of dishonorable intentions, dressed up to sound pious and holy in order to deceive you. This is my final word: from this point forward, I do not want you wasting any of your free time talking with Lord Hamlet. See to it. Come along.

4.9.oldText: HAMLET. The King is up drinking tonight, keeping the party going with noisy celebration. Every time he drains a glass of wine, the kettledrum and trumpet blast out a salute.

4.11.oldText: HAMLET. Yes, it is. And though I was born here and grew up with it, it's a custom I think is better broken than observed. This heavy drinking, known east and west, makes other nations call us drunkards and tarnish our reputation. And it does take the substance away from our real achievements, no matter how great they are. The same thing often happens with individual people — when they have some natural flaw they were born with, through no fault of their own, or some excessive tendency that overwhelms their reason, or some habit that corrupts their manners — these men, carrying the mark of a single defect, whether given by nature or by fortune, no matter how virtuous they are otherwise — as pure as grace itself, as capable as any person can be — will be condemned by public opinion because of that one particular fault. A drop of evil can ruin the noblest character.

4.14.oldText: HAMLET. Angels and ministers of grace, defend us! Whether you are a good spirit or a demon, whether you bring air from heaven or fire from hell, whether your intentions are wicked or kind — you come in such a familiar shape that I will speak to you. I'll call you Hamlet, King, father, royal Dane. Answer me! Don't let me die in ignorance. Tell me — why have your sacred bones, sealed in death, burst from their burial wrappings? Why has the tomb where we saw you laid to rest opened its heavy marble jaws to throw you back among us? What does it mean that you, a dead body, dressed again in full armor, revisit the moonlit world, making the night terrible and shaking us so deeply with thoughts beyond our understanding? Tell me — why? What should we do?

4.21.oldText: HAMLET. Why not? What is there to fear? I don't value my life at a penny's worth. And as for my soul — what can it do to that? My soul is as immortal as the ghost itself. It's waving me forward again. I'll follow it.

4.27.oldText: HAMLET. My destiny is calling, and every vein in my body is as strong as a lion's sinew.

5.4.oldText: GHOST. My time is almost up. Soon I must return to the tormenting fires of purgatory.

5.10.oldText: GHOST. I am your father's spirit, condemned for a time to walk the earth at night and burn in fires by day, until the sins of my mortal life are purged away. If I weren't forbidden to reveal the secrets of my prison, I could tell you a story whose mildest word would freeze your blood, make your eyes bulge from their sockets, and make every hair on your head stand on end like the quills of a porcupine. But these eternal mysteries are not for mortal ears. Listen — listen! If you ever loved your father —

5.15.oldText: HAMLET. Tell me quickly, so I can fly to my revenge as fast as thought itself or the wings of love.

5.16.oldText: GHOST. I see you're ready. You'd have to be duller than the lazy weed rotting on the banks of the river of forgetfulness to not be stirred by this. Now listen, Hamlet. The official story is that a serpent stung me while I slept in my orchard. All of Denmark has been grossly deceived by this false account of my death. But know this, noble young man: the serpent that stung your father now wears his crown.

5.18.oldText: GHOST. Yes, that incestuous, adulterous beast. With the witchcraft of his cleverness and his treacherous charm — oh, wicked wit and gifts that have the power to seduce! — he won over the desires of my seemingly virtuous queen. Oh Hamlet, what a collapse that was! From me, whose love was so devoted that it matched every vow I made to her in marriage, to decline to a wretch whose natural abilities were so inferior to mine. But just as virtue can never be corrupted, even when lust courts it in the form of an angel, so lust — even when linked to a shining angel — will eventually grow tired of a heavenly partner and feed on garbage. But wait — I think I sense the morning air. Let me be brief. While I was sleeping in my orchard, as I always did in the afternoon, your uncle crept up on me with a vial of poisonous liquid and poured it into my ears. The poison works so violently against human blood that it races through the body like quicksilver, curdling the blood like acid dropped into milk. That's what it did to me — and instantly, a horrible crust covered my entire body, like a leper's skin. So I was robbed — while sleeping, by my own brother's hand — of my life, my crown, and my queen, all at once. Cut off in the fullness of my sins, without confession, without communion, without last rites — sent to face my judgment with all my imperfections still on my head. Oh horrible! Oh horrible! Most horrible! If you have any natural feeling, don't let this stand. Don't let the royal bed of Denmark become a couch for lust and damned incest. But however you pursue this act, don't let your mind be corrupted, and don't plot anything against your mother. Leave her to heaven and to the thorns of guilt that will prick and sting her conscience. Farewell now! The glowworm shows that morning is near and begins to fade its pale light. Goodbye, goodbye, goodbye. Remember me.

5.20.oldText: HAMLET. Oh, all you powers of heaven! Oh earth! What else? Should I call on hell too? No! Hold together, my heart. And you, my body, don't suddenly grow weak — hold me up. Remember you? Yes, you poor ghost, as long as memory exists in this troubled mind. Remember you? Yes — I'll wipe away from my memory every trivial record, every lesson from books, every impression that youth and experience have written there. Your command alone shall live in the pages of my brain, unmixed with lesser things. Yes, by heaven! Oh, most treacherous woman! Oh villain, villain, smiling damned villain! Let me write this down — that a man may smile and smile and still be a villain. At least I'm sure that's true in Denmark.

5.22.oldText: HAMLET. So, uncle, there you are. Now, my promise: 'Goodbye, goodbye, remember me.' I have sworn it. HORATIO and MARCELLUS. [Within.] My lord! My lord!

5.39.oldText: HAMLET. You're right, you're absolutely right. And so, without any further discussion, I think it's best that we shake hands and go our separate ways — you back to whatever business you have, since every man has his business — and as for me, I think I'll go pray.

5.53.oldText: HAMLET. Ha! You hear that, do you? Are you there, old friend? Come on — you can hear this fellow down in the basement. Agree to swear.

5.57.oldText: HAMLET. Here and everywhere? Then we'll change our position. Come here, gentlemen, and put your hands on my sword again. Never to speak of what you've heard. Swear on my sword.

5.59.oldText: HAMLET. Well done, old mole! You can burrow through the earth fast! A fine digger! Let's move again, friends.

5.60.oldText: HORATIO. Good God, this is unbelievably strange.

5.61.oldText: HAMLET. Then welcome it as something strange. There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio, than are dreamt of in your philosophy. But come — here, as before, never — so help you God — no matter how strange or oddly I may behave from now on — as I may find it necessary to put on a show of madness — you must never, at such times, fold your arms like this, or shake your head, or say something vague like 'Well, we know,' or 'We could say something if we wanted to,' or 'If we chose to speak,' or 'There are people who could tell you' — or any other hint that you know anything about me. This you must not do. So help you God's grace and mercy, swear.

5.63.oldText: HAMLET. Rest, rest, troubled spirit. So, gentlemen, with all my love I entrust myself to you. And whatever poor Hamlet can do to show his love and friendship to you, God willing, he will do. Let's go in together, and remember — keep your fingers on your lips. The world has gone wrong. Oh, what a cursed fate, that I was ever born to set it right! No — come, let's go together.

6.5.oldText: POLONIUS. Good, very good. Look, sir — first find out which Danes are in Paris, how they live, who they associate with, where they stay, what they spend, and what company they keep. By circling around the topic with indirect questions, if you find that they know my son, you'll learn more than by asking directly. Pretend you have a distant acquaintance with him — like, 'I know his father and his friends, and I sort of know him.' Do you follow me, Reynaldo?

6.9.oldText: POLONIUS. Sure — or drinking, fencing, swearing, fighting, visiting women. You can go that far.

6.11.oldText: POLONIUS. Not at all — if you present it the right way. Don't make him sound like a complete degenerate — that's not what I mean. Just hint at his faults delicately enough that they sound like the natural overflow of a spirited young man — a wildness in hot young blood that everyone experiences.

6.15.oldText: POLONIUS. Here's my strategy, and I think it's a clever one. By casting these little aspersions on my son — making him sound slightly rough around the edges — the person you're talking to, if they've ever seen the young man guilty of the things you mention, will agree with you and say something like, 'Yes, sir,' or 'friend,' or 'gentleman' — depending on the person and their manner of speaking.

6.17.oldText: POLONIUS. And then, sir, he does this — he does — what was I about to say? Good grief, I was about to say something. Where did I leave off?

6.19.oldText: POLONIUS. At 'agrees with you' — yes, exactly! He agrees with you like this: 'I know the gentleman. I saw him yesterday, or the day before, or then, with so-and-so. And, as you say, he was gambling, or I caught him drunk, or I saw him get into a fight at tennis,' or maybe, 'I saw him go into a certain house' — meaning a brothel. You see? Your bait of false accusations catches the fish of truth. And this is how wise, far-reaching people use indirect methods to find out the truth. That's my lesson and my advice — use it to check on my son. You understand?

6.25.oldText: POLONIUS. And let him enjoy his music.

6.33.oldText: OPHELIA. My lord, I was sewing in my room when Lord Hamlet came in — his jacket all unfastened, no hat on his head, his stockings dirty and falling down to his ankles, pale as his shirt, his knees knocking together, and with a look on his face so full of misery that he seemed to have escaped from hell itself to tell of horrors. He came right up to me.

6.37.oldText: OPHELIA. He grabbed my wrist and held me tight. Then he stretched his arm out full length and, with his other hand over his brow, studied my face as if he were trying to draw it. He stood like that for a long time. Finally, with a little shake of my arm and three slow nods of his head, he let out a sigh so deep and pitiful it seemed to shatter his whole body. Then he let me go. He turned his head to look back at me over his shoulder and seemed to find his way out without using his eyes, because he kept them fixed on me until the very end.

6.38.oldText: POLONIUS. Come with me — I'm going to see the King. This is the madness of love, a violent passion that destroys itself and drives the will to desperate acts. I'm sorry — have you been harsh with him lately?

6.40.oldText: POLONIUS. That's what drove him mad. I'm sorry I didn't judge the situation better. I was afraid he was just playing with you and meant to ruin you. But curse my suspicion! It seems that as we get older, we tend to overthink things, just as young people tend to be rash. Come, let's go to the King. This must be made known — keeping it secret could cause more harm than revealing it.

7.1.oldText: KING. Welcome, dear Rosencrantz and Guildenstern. Beyond our great desire to see you, the need to use your help prompted us to send for you so urgently. You've heard something about Hamlet's transformation — I call it that, since neither his outer manner nor his inner self resembles what it was. What could have put him so far out of sorts, other than his father's death, I can't imagine. I ask you both — since you grew up with him and are so familiar with his personality and habits — to spend some time here at our court and draw him toward enjoyable activities, while gathering whatever information you can about whether something we don't know about is troubling him, so that we might be able to help.

7.2.oldText: QUEEN. Good gentlemen, he's talked about you often, and I'm sure there's no one alive he's more attached to. If you'd be kind enough to spend some time with us, your visit will receive the kind of thanks that befits a king's gratitude.

7.7.oldText: GUILDENSTERN. May heaven make our presence helpful to him.

7.12.oldText: KING. You've always been a bearer of good news.

7.13.oldText: POLONIUS. Have I, my lord? I assure you, I hold my duty as sacred as my soul, both to God and to my gracious King. And I believe — unless my mind has lost its skill at following political matters — that I have found the real cause of Hamlet's madness.

7.20.oldText: KING. Well, we'll get to the bottom of it.

7.23.oldText: VOLTEMAND. He sends his warmest greetings and regards. When we first raised the issue, he sent out to suppress his nephew's military buildup, which he initially thought was directed against Poland. But upon closer investigation, he discovered it was aimed at your Majesty. Distressed that his illness, age, and weakness had been taken advantage of, he had Fortinbras arrested. Fortinbras obeyed, received a rebuke from Norway, and finally swore before his uncle never to take up arms against your Majesty again. The old king, overjoyed, gave Fortinbras three thousand crowns a year and permission to use those same troops against Poland instead. He requests, as detailed here —

7.28.oldText: POLONIUS. That business is settled nicely. Now, my lord and madam — to waste time explaining what majesty is, what duty is, why day is day and night is night, would be nothing but a waste of time. Therefore, since brevity is the soul of wit, and long-windedness is mere decoration, I'll be brief: your noble son is mad. Mad, I call it, because what is true madness but being completely mad? But enough of that.

7.30.oldText: POLONIUS. Madam, I swear I'm using no style at all. That he is mad is true. It's true and it's a pity. And it's a pity it's true — that's a silly way to put it, but forget the clever phrasing, because I'm not trying to be clever. Let's agree he's mad, then. Now the question is: what's causing it? Because this faulty effect has a cause. Here's what remains. Consider this: I have a daughter — mine while she's mine — who, out of duty and obedience, has given me this. Now listen and draw your conclusions.

7.38.oldText: POLONIUS. 'Doubt that the stars are fire, Doubt that the sun moves, Doubt that truth itself is a liar, But never doubt that I love. Oh dear Ophelia, I'm bad at writing poetry. I don't have the skill to express my feelings in verse. But believe that I love you best — oh, the very best, believe it. Goodbye. Yours forever, most dear lady, as long as this body is his to give, HAMLET.' My daughter showed me this out of obedience. And beyond this, she's told me about all his romantic approaches — when, how, and where they happened.

7.42.oldText: POLONIUS. I'd like to prove that I am. But what would you think if, when I first noticed this burning love — and I noticed it, I must tell you, before my daughter told me — what would you or the Queen here think if I had just ignored it, or looked the other way, or stayed silent? What would you think? No — I went straight to work and told my young lady: 'Lord Hamlet is a prince, far above your reach. This cannot happen.' And I ordered her to refuse his company, reject his messages, and accept no gifts. She obeyed, and he — rejected — fell into sadness, then stopped eating, then couldn't sleep, then grew weak, then delirious, and finally into the madness that now has him raving — which is what we're all so worried about.

7.47.oldText: POLONIUS. I'll stake my head on it.

7.49.oldText: POLONIUS. If the evidence leads me, I'll find where the truth is hiding, even if it's buried deep.

7.51.oldText: POLONIUS. You know he sometimes walks in this hallway for hours at a time.

7.53.oldText: POLONIUS. At one of those times, I'll send my daughter to him. You and I will hide behind a curtain and observe the encounter. If he doesn't love her, and that's not what's driving him mad, then I'll give up my position and go tend a farm.

7.68.oldText: HAMLET. Because if the sun can breed maggots in a dead dog — do you have a daughter?

7.73.oldText: POLONIUS. What's it about, my lord?

7.76.oldText: HAMLET. Slander, sir. This satirical writer claims that old men have grey beards, wrinkled faces, eyes oozing thick goo, and a severe lack of intelligence, along with very weak legs. All of which, sir, I believe with absolute conviction, yet I think it's rude to put it in print. Because you yourself, sir, would be as old as I am if, like a crab, you could walk backwards.

7.77.oldText: POLONIUS. [Aside.] Though this is madness, there's a method to it. — Would you like to step out of this drafty hallway, my lord?

7.79.oldText: POLONIUS. Indeed, that would be out of the draft. [Aside.] How sharp his replies are sometimes! That's a kind of insight that madness often stumbles onto, which sanity couldn't produce so neatly. I'll leave him now and immediately arrange a meeting between him and my daughter. — My lord, I'll take my humble leave of you.

7.91.oldText: GUILDENSTERN. Happy enough — not too happy. We're not at the top of Fortune's wheel.

7.96.oldText: HAMLET. In Fortune's most private parts? Oh yes, she is a fickle mistress. What's the news?

7.110.oldText: HAMLET. Then beggars are the real solid beings, and monarchs and heroes are just beggars' shadows. Shall we go to court? I'm not reasoning very well. ROSENCRANTZ and GUILDENSTERN. We'll attend you.

7.115.oldText: HAMLET. Anything — just tell the truth. You were sent for, and there's a kind of confession in your faces that you're not clever enough to hide. I know the King and Queen sent for you.

7.121.oldText: HAMLET. I'll tell you why, so you won't have to reveal what the King and Queen told you. I have lately — though I don't know why — lost all my enjoyment, given up all my usual activities. Everything feels so heavy that this magnificent earth seems to me like a barren wasteland. This beautiful canopy of sky — this magnificent overhanging firmament, this majestic roof decorated with golden fire — it all looks like nothing more than a foul, pestilent collection of fumes. What a piece of work is man! How noble in reason, how infinite in ability! In form and movement, how precise and admirable! In action, like an angel! In understanding, like a god! The beauty of the world, the masterpiece of all living things. And yet, to me, what is this ultimate distillation of dust? Man gives me no delight — nor woman either, though your smiling suggests you think otherwise.

7.124.oldText: ROSENCRANTZ. I was thinking, my lord, that if you have no delight in man, what a poor reception the actors will get from you. We passed them on the road — they're on their way here to perform for you.

7.125.oldText: HAMLET. The one who plays the king will be welcome — his Majesty will get tribute from me. The adventurous knight can use his sword and shield. The lover won't sigh for nothing. The comedian can finish his part in peace. The clown will make the easy laughers laugh. And the lady can speak her mind freely, or the rhythm will suffer. What company is it?

7.132.oldText: ROSENCRANTZ. No, they work as hard as ever. But there's a troupe of child actors — little hawks — who screech louder than anyone and get wildly applauded for it. They're the fashion now, and they've so ridiculed the regular theaters that many grown actors are afraid of being satirized and hardly dare perform anymore.

7.134.oldText: ROSENCRANTZ. Actually, there's been a lot of controversy on both sides, and the public thinks it's great entertainment to egg them on. For a while, no one would invest in a play unless the playwright and the actors were fighting about it.

7.136.oldText: GUILDENSTERN. Oh, there's been plenty of intellectual battling.

7.138.oldText: ROSENCRANTZ. They do, my lord — they've even taken on the biggest names.

7.139.oldText: HAMLET. That's not so strange, really. My uncle is King of Denmark, and people who used to mock him while my father was alive now pay forty or fifty ducats for a miniature portrait of him. There's something unnatural in all this, if philosophy could figure it out.

7.147.oldText: HAMLET. Listen, Guildenstern — and you too, lean in. That big baby you see there hasn't outgrown his swaddling clothes yet.

7.156.oldText: POLONIUS. They're the best actors in the world — for tragedy, comedy, history, pastoral, pastoral-comical, historical-pastoral, tragical-historical, tragical-comical-historical-pastoral, continuous drama, or anything without rules. No one can be too heavy or too light for them. They're the only company worth seeing.

7.165.oldText: HAMLET. Why — 'As fate would have it,' and then, you know, 'It came to pass, as was most likely.' The first verse of the old song will tell you more. But look — here comes my entertainment.

7.167.oldText: HAMLET. Welcome, all of you! I'm glad to see you well. Welcome, good friends. Oh, my old friend! Your face has grown a beard since I saw you last — are you here to challenge me in Denmark? And my young lady! By heaven, your ladyship has grown taller since I last saw you — a good few inches closer to heaven. I hope your voice, like a coin, hasn't cracked out of circulation. Welcome, everyone. Let's get right to it, like eager falconers chasing anything that flies. Give us a speech right now — a passionate one.

7.169.oldText: HAMLET. I once heard you deliver a speech that was never performed publicly — or if it was, only once, because the play didn't appeal to the masses. It was caviar to the general public. But it was — as I and others whose judgment I respect agreed — an excellent play, well-structured, written with skill and restraint. Someone said it had no crude jokes to spice things up and no pretentious language that would make the author seem affected, but called it an honest, well-crafted work — as wholesome as it was elegant, and much more substantial than flashy. There was one speech in it I especially loved — Aeneas's tale to Dido, particularly the part about Priam's slaughter. If you remember it, start from this line — let me think — 'The savage Pyrrhus, like the Hyrcanian beast' — no, that's not it. It starts with Pyrrhus. 'The savage Pyrrhus — he whose dark arms, black as his murderous purpose, matched the night when he lay hidden in the wooden horse — now has his dreadful, dark complexion smeared with even more terrible markings. From head to foot he is drenched in red, horribly splashed with the blood of fathers, mothers, daughters, and sons, baked and crusted by the burning streets that cast a tyrannical, hellish light on their vile murders. Roasted in fury and fire, coated with clotted gore, with eyes like burning coals, the hellish Pyrrhus seeks old Priam.' Go on from there.

7.170.oldText: POLONIUS. That was well spoken, my lord — good delivery and good feeling.

7.171.oldText: FIRST PLAYER. Soon he finds him, striking uselessly at Greeks. His ancient sword, too heavy for his old arm, falls where it lands, refusing to obey him. In an unequal fight, Pyrrhus drives at Priam, striking wide in his fury. But just the rush of wind from his terrible sword knocks the feeble old man down. Then the very walls of Troy seemed to feel this blow, and the flaming rooftop crashed down with a hideous noise, freezing Pyrrhus in his tracks. For look — his sword, which was about to fall on Priam's white-haired head, seemed to stick in the air. Like a painted figure, Pyrrhus stood motionless, suspended between his will and his action, doing nothing. But just as we often see before a storm — silence in the heavens, the clouds standing still, the wild winds speechless, the world below as quiet as death — and then suddenly the terrible thunder rips through the sky — so, after that pause, fresh vengeance drove Pyrrhus back to his work. And never did the giant Cyclops's hammers fall on the god of war's eternal armor with less mercy than Pyrrhus's bloody sword now fell on Priam. Down, down with you, fickle Fortune! All you gods, take away her power! Break the wheel she spins! And hurl it down from the heights of heaven to the depths of hell!

7.174.oldText: FIRST PLAYER. 'But who — oh, who — had seen the grief-stricken queen —'

7.176.oldText: POLONIUS. That's good! 'Grief-stricken queen' is good.

7.177.oldText: FIRST PLAYER. Running barefoot through the streets, threatening the flames with blinding tears. A rag upon her head where the crown once sat, and for a robe, a blanket snatched up in panic around her exhausted body — anyone who had seen her, with a tongue dipped in venom, would have called Fortune a traitor. But if the gods themselves had seen her — when she saw Pyrrhus savagely hacking her husband's body to pieces — the shriek she let out, unless nothing mortal could move them, would have brought tears to the burning eyes of heaven and stirred passion in the gods.

7.179.oldText: HAMLET. Fine. I'll have you finish the rest soon. — Good my lord, will you see that the players are well taken care of? Treat them well — they are the mirrors and brief chronicles of the age. You'd rather have a bad epitaph after your death than their bad review while you're alive.

7.194.oldText: HAMLET. Right then — goodbye. Now I'm alone. Oh, what a worthless, pathetic slave I am! Isn't it incredible that this actor, working with nothing but fiction — a fantasy of emotion — could force his soul into such sympathy with his role that his face went pale, tears came to his eyes, his voice broke, and his whole body shaped itself to match his feeling? And all for nothing! For Hecuba! What's Hecuba to him, or he to Hecuba, that he should weep for her? What would he do if he had the motive and the cause for passion that I have? He'd drown the stage in tears and shatter every ear with terrifying speech, drive the guilty mad, horrify the innocent, confuse the ignorant, and overwhelm the very powers of sight and hearing. Yet here I am — a dull, spiritless coward — moping around like a daydreamer, indifferent to my cause, unable to say a word. Not a word — for a king whose life and throne were stolen through damned treachery. Am I a coward? Who calls me a villain? Who slaps me across the face? Pulls my beard? Tweaks my nose? Calls me a liar to my face? Who does this to me? I should take it, because I must be coward-hearted, lacking the gall to fight back — otherwise I would have fed every vulture in the sky with this villain's guts by now. Bloody, lecherous, remorseless, treacherous, unnatural villain! Oh, revenge! But why am I ranting like this? This is pathetic — that I, the son of a murdered father, urged to revenge by heaven and hell itself, must pour out my heart with words like a prostitute and curse like a kitchen maid. Shame on me! Enough! Think, brain! I've heard that guilty people watching a play have sometimes been so struck by the scene that they've confessed their crimes on the spot. Because murder, though it has no tongue, will speak through the most miraculous means. I'll have these players perform something like my father's murder in front of my uncle. I'll watch his face. I'll probe him deeply. If he even flinches, I'll know what to do. The spirit I saw may be the devil — and the devil can disguise himself in a pleasing shape. Maybe, out of my weakness and depression — since he's very powerful with such vulnerable spirits — he's trying to trick me into damning myself. I need better proof than this. The play's the thing — I'll use it to catch the conscience of the King.

8.14.oldText: KING. Dear Gertrude, leave us too. We've secretly arranged for Hamlet to come here as if by accident, where he'll run into Ophelia. Her father and I — perfectly justified in spying — will position ourselves where we can see without being seen, and openly judge from his behavior whether it's the affliction of love or something else that's making him suffer.

8.18.oldText: POLONIUS. Ophelia, walk here. — Your Majesty, we'll hide ourselves. — [To Ophelia.] Read this prayer book, so the appearance of devotion can explain why you're alone here. It's something we're often guilty of — putting on a pious face to cover up devilish intentions.

8.19.oldText: KING. [Aside.] How painfully true that is! Those words sting my conscience. The painted cheek of a prostitute, covered in makeup, is no uglier compared to what's beneath it than my actions are compared to my fine-sounding words. What a heavy burden!

8.23.oldText: HAMLET. To be, or not to be — that is the question. Is it nobler to endure the attacks and insults of outrageous fortune, or to take up arms against a sea of troubles and, by fighting, end them? To die — to sleep, nothing more. And by sleeping, to say we end the heartache and the thousand natural shocks that human flesh is subject to — that's a conclusion devoutly to be wished for. To die, to sleep. To sleep — and maybe to dream. Yes, there's the problem. Because in that sleep of death, what dreams might come after we've shed this mortal body must give us pause. That's what makes us endure misery for so long. For who would bear the whips and insults of time — the oppressor's cruelty, the proud man's contempt, the agony of unreturned love, the slowness of the law, the arrogance of those in power, and the abuse that patient, deserving people take from the unworthy — when he could simply end it all with a dagger? Who would carry these burdens, grunting and sweating under a weary life, if it weren't for the dread of something after death — that undiscovered country from which no traveler returns? That fear confuses our will and makes us endure the miseries we know rather than rush toward unknown ones. And so our conscience makes cowards of us all. The natural color of courage gets sickened over with the pale cast of too much thinking, and plans of great importance lose their momentum and never become action. But wait — here comes the beautiful Ophelia! — In your prayers, remember all my sins.

8.28.oldText: OPHELIA. My lord, you know very well you did. And with them came words so sweetly spoken that they made the gifts more precious. Now that sweetness is gone — take them back. To a noble mind, rich gifts lose their value when the giver proves unkind. Here, my lord.

8.35.oldText: HAMLET. Absolutely — because the power of beauty will corrupt virtue into something base sooner than virtue can make beauty honest. That used to be a paradox, but now our times prove it. I did love you once.

8.37.oldText: HAMLET. You shouldn't have believed me. Virtue can't purify our corrupt nature completely — we'll always taste the original sin. I did not love you.

8.45.oldText: HAMLET. I've heard all about your painting too — how God gives you one face and you make yourselves another. You dance, you sway, you talk in that affected way, and you give cute nicknames to God's creatures, and you pretend your wanton behavior is just innocence. Enough — it's driven me mad. I tell you, there will be no more marriages. Those who are already married — all but one — shall live. The rest will stay single. To a convent, go.

8.47.oldText: OPHELIA. Oh, what a noble mind has been destroyed! The perfect courtier, soldier, and scholar — the hope and ornament of our country, the mirror of fashion, the model of form, the one everyone watched and admired — completely, completely ruined! And I, the most miserable of women, who drank the honey of his beautiful promises — now I see that noble and supreme reason jangling like broken bells, harsh and out of tune. That matchless form and spirit of glowing youth, blasted by madness. Oh, what misery, to have seen what I once saw and now see what I see.

9.1.oldText: HAMLET. Deliver the speech, please, the way I taught it to you — naturally and smoothly. But if you start shouting it, I'd just as soon have the town crier read my lines. And don't wave your arms around too much — use restraint. Even in the middle of the most powerful storm of emotion, you must find a smoothness and control. It pains me to hear some blustering, wig-wearing fellow tear a speech to shreds, splitting the ears of the audience, who mostly can only appreciate pointless spectacle and noise. I'd have such a man whipped for overacting. It out-Herods Herod. Please avoid that.

9.3.oldText: HAMLET. But don't be too tame either. Let your own good judgment guide you. Match the action to the words and the words to the action, with this one rule: don't overdo it. Because anything overdone defeats the whole purpose of acting, which has always been to hold a mirror up to nature — to show virtue its own reflection, foolishness its own image, and each era its true character. Now, if you overdo it or underplay it, even though it might make ignorant people laugh, it will make anyone with taste groan — and the opinion of one such person should outweigh that of a whole theater of others. There are actors I've seen — and heard praised highly — who, not to put too fine a point on it, didn't walk, talk, or behave like Christians, or even like human beings, but strutted and bellowed so badly that I thought some of nature's less talented craftsmen must have made them, they imitated humanity so poorly.

9.5.oldText: HAMLET. Correct it completely. And make sure the comedians stick to their scripts. Some of them will start improvising to get cheap laughs from the dullest part of the audience, right when something important is happening in the play. That's contemptible, and shows a pathetic kind of ambition in the fool who does it. Go get ready.

9.19.oldText: HAMLET. No, don't think I'm flattering you. What could I possibly gain from you? You have no income, nothing but your good character to sustain you. Why would anyone flatter a poor man? No — let fawning tongues lick the boots of absurd power and bend their knees wherever there's profit in groveling. Listen to me: ever since my soul was capable of choosing its friends, it has chosen you. Because you have been a person who, while enduring everything, suffers nothing — a man who has taken both the blows and the gifts of fortune with equal grace. Blessed are those whose emotions and judgment are so well balanced that they are not a pipe for fortune to play whatever tune she pleases on. Give me a man who is not a slave to his emotions, and I will hold him in my heart of hearts — as I hold you. But enough of that. There's a play tonight before the King. One scene in it closely mirrors the circumstances of my father's death, as I told you. Please, when you see that scene, watch my uncle with the sharpest attention of your soul. If his hidden guilt doesn't reveal itself during one particular speech, then the ghost we saw was a devil, and my suspicions are as foul as a blacksmith's forge. Watch him closely — I'll have my eyes locked on his face — and afterward we'll compare our judgments.

9.20.oldText: HORATIO. My lord, if he steals any reaction during this play and I miss it, I'll pay the price.

9.22.oldText: [Danish march. A flourish. Enter King, Queen, Polonius, Ophelia,]

9.25.oldText: HAMLET. Excellently, thank you — I eat nothing but air, stuffed full of promises. You can't feed chickens like that.

9.26.oldText: KING. I don't know what to make of that answer, Hamlet. Those words mean nothing to me.

9.27.oldText: HAMLET. Nor to me, anymore. [To Polonius.] My lord, you once acted in a university play, you say?

9.34.oldText: HAMLET. No, good mother — here's something more attractive.

9.43.oldText: HAMLET. That's a good thing to have between a girl's legs.

9.51.oldText: HAMLET. That long? Well then, let the devil wear black — I'll have a suit of fine fur. Heavens — dead two months and not forgotten yet? Then there's hope that a great man's memory can outlive his life by half a year. But he'd better build churches, or else nobody will think of him at all — just like the hobby-horse, whose motto is 'The hobby-horse is forgotten!'

9.53.oldText: [Enter a King and a Queen very lovingly; the Queen embracing him and he her. She kneels, and makes show of protestation unto him. He takes her up, and declines his head upon her neck. Lays him down upon a bank of flowers. She, seeing him asleep, leaves him. Anon comes in a fellow, takes off his crown, kisses it, pours poison in the King's ears, and exits. The Queen returns, finds the King dead, and makes passionate action. The Poisoner with some three or four Mutes, comes in again, seeming to lament with her. The dead body is carried away. The Poisoner woos the Queen with gifts. She seems loth and unwilling awhile, but in the end accepts his love]

9.56.oldText: HAMLET. It means mischief — sneaky mischief.

9.62.oldText: OPHELIA. You're naughty. I'll just watch the play.

9.63.oldText: PROLOGUE. To you and to our play, here kneeling humbly, we beg your patient hearing.

9.68.oldText: PLAYER KING. Thirty times has the sun made its circuit around the salty seas and the round earth, and thirty dozen moons have lit the world twelve times thirty nights, since love joined our hearts and marriage joined our hands in sacred union.

9.69.oldText: PLAYER QUEEN. May we count as many more journeys of the sun and moon before our love is done. But I'm so worried about you — you've been so ill lately, so changed from your former self, that I'm filled with fear. Yet my worry must not distress you, my lord. A woman's fear and love are proportional — either both are nothing, or both are everything. My love has proven itself, and my fear matches it. Where love is great, even the smallest doubts feel enormous. Where fears are small, love has room to grow.

9.75.oldText: PLAYER QUEEN. May the earth give me no food and heaven no light. May rest and comfort flee from me day and night. May hope turn to despair, and prison be my home. May every opposite of joy destroy what I wish for! May I suffer endlessly, here and in the afterlife, if I ever marry again after becoming a widow.

9.79.oldText: PLAYER QUEEN. Sleep peacefully, and may nothing bad ever come between us.

9.82.oldText: QUEEN. The lady protests too much, I think.

9.87.oldText: HAMLET. The Mousetrap. How's that for a title? Metaphorically, of course. This play depicts a murder committed in Vienna. Gonzago is the duke's name; his wife is Baptista. You'll see soon enough. It's a wicked piece of work — but so what? Your Majesty and those of us with clear consciences have nothing to worry about. Let the guilty horse wince — we have nothing to hide.

9.90.oldText: OPHELIA. You make a good narrator, my lord.

9.95.oldText: HAMLET. That's how women take their husbands — for better and worse. — Begin, murderer! Enough with the ugly faces — get on with it. Come on — the raven croaks for revenge.

9.96.oldText: LUCIANUS. Thoughts black, hands ready, poison prepared, and the moment right — with no witnesses, and the season as my accomplice. You vile mixture, brewed from midnight weeds, three times cursed and three times infected — let your deadly nature seize this wholesome life immediately.

9.100.oldText: HAMLET. What — frightened by a stage trick?

9.105.oldText: HAMLET. Well! Let the wounded deer weep while the unharmed deer plays. Some must watch while others sleep — that's the way the world goes. Wouldn't this performance, sir, plus a feathered hat, if my other fortunes turned on me — with a couple of fancy roses on my shoes — earn me a spot in a troupe of actors?

9.107.oldText: HAMLET. A whole one, I'd say! For you know, dear friend, this kingdom was stripped of its rightful ruler, and now a mere — peacock — reigns here.

9.113.oldText: HAMLET. Yes! Come, let's have some music! Bring the recorders! Because if the King doesn't like the comedy, well then — I guess he just doesn't like it. Come, some music!

9.121.oldText: GUILDENSTERN. No, my lord — from anger.

9.127.oldText: GUILDENSTERN. No, my lord — this politeness isn't what's needed. If you'll give me a straight answer, I'll carry out your mother's request. If not, your forgiveness and my departure will end our business.

9.130.oldText: HAMLET. Give you a straight answer — my mind is unwell. But I'll give you the best answer I can — or rather, as you say, what my mother wants. So, no more preamble. My mother, you say —

9.136.oldText: HAMLET. And I still do, I swear by these honest hands.

9.139.oldText: ROSENCRANTZ. How can that be, when the King himself has named you as his successor in Denmark?

9.142.oldText: HAMLET. Oh — the recorders. Let me see one. — Now, why are you circling around me like hunters trying to drive me into a trap?

9.152.oldText: HAMLET. Well, look at how little you think of me! You'd play on me — you'd pretend to know my inner workings, you'd pluck out the heart of my mystery, you'd sound me from my lowest note to my highest — and yet there is excellent music and voice in this little instrument, and you can't make it speak. Do you think I'm easier to play than a pipe? Call me whatever instrument you like — though you can irritate me, you cannot play me.

9.157.oldText: POLONIUS. By heaven, it does look like a camel.

9.159.oldText: POLONIUS. It does have a weasel-like shape.

10.3.oldText: ROSENCRANTZ. Every individual person is duty-bound to protect themselves with all their mental strength and will. But how much more so the person upon whose well-being so many other lives depend. When a king falls, it's like a massive wheel fixed to the highest peak — when it falls, every small thing attached to it comes crashing down too. A king never sighs alone — it causes a universal groan.

10.10.oldText: KING. Oh, my offense is vile — it stinks to heaven. It bears the oldest curse of all — a brother's murder! I cannot pray, though my desire to pray is as sharp as my will. My stronger guilt defeats my strong intention, and, like a man pulled in two directions at once, I stand paralyzed, unable to begin, and both tasks left undone. What if this cursed hand were thicker than itself with brother's blood — isn't there enough rain in all the sweet heavens to wash it white as snow? What's the purpose of mercy if not to confront the face of sin? And what is prayer's power if not this double force: to prevent us from falling, or to pardon us once we've fallen? Then I'll look up. My sin is in the past. But oh — what form of prayer can help me? 'Forgive me my foul murder'? That cannot be, since I still possess everything I murdered to get — my crown, my ambition, and my queen. Can a person be pardoned while still holding the profits of the crime? In the corrupt currents of this world, a criminal's gold-tipped hand can push justice aside, and often the stolen prize itself buys off the law. But it's not that way in heaven. There, you can't cheat — the case is tried in its true nature, and we are forced to confront our faults face to face and give testimony against ourselves. What then? What's left? Try what repentance can do. What can't it do? Yet what use is it when one cannot repent? Oh, wretched state! Oh, heart as black as death! Oh, soul trapped like a bird in lime — the more you struggle to be free, the more tangled you become! Help, angels! Let me try. Bow, stubborn knees, and heart with strings of steel, become as soft as a newborn baby's. All may yet be well.

10.13.oldText: HAMLET. Now I could do it — right now, while he's praying. And now I'll do it. And so he goes straight to heaven. And that's my revenge? That needs more thought. A villain murders my father, and for that I, his only son, send that same villain to heaven. No — that's a reward, not revenge. He killed my father while my father was unprepared — full of earthly pleasures, with all his sins in full bloom. And what his account looks like before God, only heaven knows — but by our way of thinking, it weighs heavily against him. And would it be revenge to kill him while he's purifying his soul, when he's prepared and ready for death? No. Sword, wait for a more terrible opportunity: when he's passed out drunk, or in a rage, or in the pleasure of his incestuous bed, or gambling, or swearing, or doing something that has no trace of salvation in it. Then strike him down, so his heels may kick at heaven and his soul be as damned and black as hell, where it will go. My mother is waiting. This praying only extends your numbered days.

10.15.oldText: HAMLET. The King rises and advances.

11.19.oldText: HAMLET. What? A rat? [Draws his sword.] Dead, for a dollar — dead!

11.23.oldText: QUEEN. Oh God, what have you done?

11.29.oldText: HAMLET. Yes, lady, that's what I said. — [To Polonius.] You wretched, rash, meddling fool — farewell! I mistook you for your superior. Accept your fate — you've learned that being too nosy is dangerous. — Stop wringing your hands. Sit down and let me wring your heart, because I will — if it hasn't grown so hardened by wicked habit that it's impervious to feeling.

11.33.oldText: HAMLET. Look at this picture, and now at this — portraits of two brothers. See what grace sat on this brow — the curls of a sun god, the forehead of Jove himself, eyes like Mars commanding with authority, a bearing like Mercury, the winged messenger of the gods, newly landed on a heaven-kissing hill. A combination where every god seemed to set his seal, guaranteeing the world: this is a man. This was your husband. Now look at the next one. Here is your husband — like a diseased ear of corn, blighting his wholesome brother. Do you have eyes? Could you leave this beautiful mountain to graze in this swamp? Do you have eyes? You can't call it love — at your age, passion has calmed down and waits upon judgment. And what kind of judgment would step from this to that? Your senses must be paralyzed — because even madness wouldn't make such an error, and no sense was ever so enslaved to insanity that it couldn't retain some ability to choose between such different options. What devil tricked you in this blindfold game? Eyes without feeling, feeling without sight, hearing without hands or eyes, smell without anything else, or even a sick fragment of one true sense, could not be so deluded. Oh shame — where is your blush? If rebellion can burn in a mature woman's bones, then let virtue melt like wax in the heat of flaming youth. Don't bother calling anything shameful when overpowering lust takes the lead, since even frost burns with equal passion, and reason becomes the servant of desire.

11.37.oldText: HAMLET. A murderer and a villain — a slave who isn't a twentieth of the man your former husband was. A clown king, a pickpocket of the empire, who stole the precious crown from its shelf and put it in his pocket!

11.46.oldText: QUEEN. How are you, rather? You're staring at empty air and talking to nothing! Your eyes are wild and staring, and your hair, like sleeping soldiers woken by an alarm, is standing straight on end. Oh, gentle son — sprinkle cool patience on the heat and flame of your madness. What are you looking at?

11.55.oldText: QUEEN. This is purely a creation of your disturbed brain. Madness is very skilled at producing these kinds of hallucinations.

11.56.oldText: HAMLET. Madness? My pulse beats as steadily as yours, keeping healthy time. What I've said is not madness. Test me — I'll repeat it word for word. Madness would scramble everything. Mother, for the love of God, don't comfort your soul with the flattering belief that it's my madness speaking and not your own guilt. That would only put a thin skin over the ulcerous wound, while the rot keeps spreading underneath. Confess to heaven. Repent what's past. Avoid what's to come. And don't fertilize the weeds to make them grow even thicker. Forgive me for this moralizing — in these bloated times, virtue itself must beg vice for permission to do good.

11.60.oldText: HAMLET. I'm sorry. But heaven has chosen to punish me through him and him through me, making me its instrument of justice. I'll take care of the body and accept responsibility for his death. So again, good night. I must be cruel only to be kind. This is a bad beginning, and worse is yet to come. One more thing, good lady.

11.62.oldText: HAMLET. Absolutely not this, which I'm telling you to do: don't let the bloated King tempt you back to bed, pinch your cheek playfully, call you his pet name, and with his damned fingers on your neck and his filthy kisses, get you to reveal everything — that I'm not truly mad, but only pretending to be mad. It would be good to let him know — because what queen, fair, sensible, and wise, would hide such important matters from a toad, a bat, a tomcat? Who would do that? No — despite all sense and secrecy, don't open the cage on the rooftop, let the birds fly out, and then, like the famous ape, climb into the cage yourself and break your own neck.

11.66.oldText: HAMLET. There are sealed letters — and my two school friends, whom I trust about as far as I'd trust venomous snakes — they carry the orders and will escort me straight into a trap. Let it happen. There's a special pleasure in seeing the bomb-maker blown up by his own bomb. And it'll be a hard day when I can't dig a yard deeper than their tunnels and blow them sky-high. Oh, it's so satisfying when two schemes collide head-on. This man will get me moving. I'll drag the body into the next room. Mother, good night. Indeed, this advisor is now very still, very secret, and very grave — though in life he was a foolish, chattering fool. Come, sir, let me wrap things up with you. Good night, mother.

12.7.oldText: KING. Oh, terrible deed! That could have been us if we had been there. His freedom is a threat to everyone — to you, to us, to the whole world. How will this bloody act be answered for? It will be blamed on us, since our love should have kept this dangerous young man restrained and out of harm's way. But we loved him so much that we refused to see what needed to be done, like the owner of a terrible disease who lets it feed on his own vitality rather than revealing it. Where has he gone?

12.9.oldText: KING. Oh Gertrude, come! As soon as the sun touches the mountains, we'll ship him away. And we must use all our authority and skill to both acknowledge and excuse this terrible act. — Guildenstern!

12.13.oldText: KING. Come, Gertrude — we'll summon our wisest advisors and tell them what we plan to do and what has happened. Perhaps that way slander — whose whisper reaches across the world as straight as a cannonball to its target, carrying its poisonous shot — may miss our name and hit only the empty air. Oh, come away! My soul is full of conflict and dread.

13.11.oldText: HAMLET. Yes, sir — one that soaks up the King's favor, his rewards, and his authority. But people like you serve the King best in the end: he keeps you, like an ape keeps food in the corner of its mouth — first chewed, then swallowed last. When he needs what you've absorbed, he just squeezes you dry.

13.13.oldText: HAMLET. I'm glad of it. A clever remark is wasted on a foolish ear.

13.17.oldText: HAMLET. Of nothing. Take me to him. Come on — hide and seek!

14.1.oldText: KING. I've sent people to find him and locate the body. How dangerous it is that this man walks free! Yet we can't apply the full force of the law — he's loved by the confused masses, who judge with their eyes and not their minds. In such cases, the offender's punishment is noticed, but never the offense itself. To keep everything smooth and even, this sudden sending away must appear to be a carefully considered decision. Desperate diseases require desperate remedies — or no remedy at all.

14.17.oldText: HAMLET. Nothing — just showing you how a king can take a journey through the guts of a beggar.

14.28.oldText: HAMLET. I see an angel who sees them. But come — off to England! Farewell, dear mother.

15.1.oldText: FORTINBRAS. Go, Captain. Give my greetings to the Danish king. Tell him that Fortinbras requests permission, as promised, to march his army across his kingdom. You know the meeting point. If his Majesty needs anything from us, we'll present ourselves to him in person. Let him know.

15.13.oldText: CAPTAIN. To tell the truth, with no exaggeration, we're going to capture a tiny patch of ground that has no value except its name. I wouldn't pay five ducats to farm it, and it wouldn't bring a better price if sold outright to Norway or Poland.

15.22.oldText: HAMLET. Everything I see accuses me and spurs on my sluggish revenge! What is a man if his greatest purpose is just sleeping and eating? A beast, nothing more. Surely the one who made us with such expansive reason — the ability to look forward and backward — didn't give us that godlike capacity just to let it rust unused. Now, whether it's animal-like forgetfulness, or some cowardly hesitation from thinking too precisely about consequences — a thought which, when examined, turns out to be one part wisdom and three parts cowardice — I don't know why I'm still alive saying 'This thing needs to be done' when I have the cause, the will, the strength, and the means to do it. Examples as plain as the earth itself urge me on. Look at this army of enormous size and expense, led by a delicate and tender prince whose spirit, swollen with divine ambition, laughs at the unforeseeable outcome, risking everything mortal and uncertain against all that fortune, death, and danger can throw at him — even for an eggshell. True greatness is not about refusing to act without a great cause, but about finding something worth fighting for even in the smallest insult, when honor is at stake. How do I stand, then — with a father murdered, a mother dishonored, provocations to both my reason and my passion — and yet I do nothing? While to my shame, I watch the imminent death of twenty thousand men who, for a fantasy and a bit of fame, march to their graves as easily as to their beds, fighting over a plot of ground too small to hold them all or even to bury the dead. From this moment on, let my thoughts be bloody or worthless.

16.4.oldText: GENTLEMAN. She talks a lot about her father. She says she hears there are plots afoot in the world. She wrings her hands, thumps her chest, is irrationally angry at trivial things, and speaks in a confused way that only half makes sense. Her speech is meaningless, yet its very confusion moves the listeners to piece it together. They try to make sense of it, and with her winks and nods and gestures, they construct meaning. It's nothing certain, but it's deeply unsettling. It would be wise to speak with her — she might plant dangerous suspicions in troubled minds.

16.12.oldText: OPHELIA. How should I tell your true love from another one? By his pilgrim's hat and his walking staff and his sandals.

16.34.oldText: OPHELIA. By Jesus and by Saint Charity, oh, the shame of it! Young men will do it if they get the chance — truly, they are to blame. She said: Before you had me, you promised me you'd wed. And he said: So I would have, by the sun above, if you hadn't come to my bed.

16.40.oldText: KING. Oh, this is the poison of deep grief — it all springs from her father's death. Oh Gertrude, Gertrude — when sorrows come, they come not one at a time, but in whole armies. First, her father killed. Then your son, gone — and he himself the violent cause of his own banishment. The people are confused, thick with unwholesome thoughts and whispers about Polonius's death. And we were foolish to bury him in such secrecy and haste. Poor Ophelia, torn away from her own mind and good judgment — without which we are nothing more than pictures or mere animals. And finally, and just as serious as all the rest: her brother has secretly returned from France. He feeds on his bewilderment, keeps to the shadows, and has no shortage of gossips buzzing in his ear with poisonous stories about his father's death. These rumors, starved for real facts, won't hesitate to blame us directly. Oh, my dear Gertrude — all of this, like a weapon packed with scattered shot, is killing me over and over.

16.43.oldText: KING. Where are my guards? Let them protect the door!

16.56.oldText: LAERTES. If there's a drop of calm blood in me, it proclaims me a bastard, calls my father a cuckold, and brands my honest mother a whore.

16.72.oldText: LAERTES. Oh God — let my brains dry up! Let tears seven times as salty burn out my sight! By heaven, her madness will be paid back in full until the scales tip in our favor! Oh rose of May! Dear girl, kind sister, sweet Ophelia! Oh heavens — is it possible that a young woman's sanity could be as fragile as an old man's life? Human nature is so refined in love that when love is intense enough, it sends some precious part of itself after the thing it loves.

16.76.oldText: OPHELIA. You have to sing 'Down a-down, and you call him a-down-a.' Oh, how the spinning wheel suits the song! It's the story of the false steward who stole his master's daughter.

16.89.oldText: LAERTES. So be it. The manner of his death, his obscure burial — no monument, no sword of honor over his bones, no noble ceremony, no proper funeral — all of this cries out to be investigated, demanding an explanation as loud as a voice from heaven to earth.

17.9.oldText: HORATIO. [Reads.] 'Horatio — when you've read this, arrange for these men to get an audience with the King. They have letters for him. We were barely two days at sea when a pirate ship, well-armed for battle, gave us chase. Finding our ship too slow, we fought back out of necessity, and during the boarding I jumped onto their vessel. The instant I did, they broke free of our ship, so I alone became their prisoner. They've treated me like merciful thieves — but they knew what they were doing. I owe them a favor in return. Make sure the King gets the letters I've sent, and come to me as fast as if you were running from death itself. I have things to tell you that will strike you dumb, yet they're not weighty enough for what this situation requires. These men will bring you to where I am. Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are still on course for England — I have much to tell you about them. Farewell. He who you know is yours, HAMLET.' Come, I'll help you deliver these letters, and quickly too, so you can then take me to the man who sent them.

18.2.oldText: LAERTES. That's clear enough. But tell me — why didn't you take action against these crimes, so serious and so deserving of punishment, when your own safety, wisdom, and every other consideration should have driven you to act?

18.3.oldText: KING. For two special reasons that may seem weak to you but are strong for me. The Queen, his mother, lives almost entirely for him. And as for myself — whether it's my virtue or my curse — she's so bound up with my life and soul that, like a star that can only move within its sphere, I can't function without her. The other reason I couldn't bring him to public trial is the great love that the common people bear for him. They dip all his faults in their affection, like a spring that turns wood to stone, converting his chains into decorations. My accusations, too lightly made against so powerful a wind of popularity, would have blown right back at me instead of hitting their target.

18.17.oldText: KING. If that's how it is, Laertes — and how could it not be? — will you let me guide you?

18.23.oldText: KING. Just a ribbon in the cap of youth, but a necessary one too — because youthful energy is as naturally suited to light and carefree attire as maturity is to dignified clothing. About two months ago, a gentleman from Normandy visited — I've fought against the French myself, and they're superb horsemen — but this fellow seemed to be made one with his horse. He was so extraordinary on horseback that I couldn't even imagine what he did, let alone describe it.

18.33.oldText: KING. Not because I doubt your love. But I know that love begins in time, and I've seen, through clear examples, that time weakens its fire. Within the very flame of love lives a kind of wick that will make it burn lower. Nothing stays good forever — goodness, when it grows too much, dies of its own excess. What we want to do, we should do when we feel like it — because 'want to' changes, and has as many delays and obstacles as there are tongues, hands, and accidents in the world. And then that 'should' becomes like a wasteful sigh — it brings relief but does damage. But let's get to the heart of the matter. Hamlet's back. What would you do to prove yourself your father's true son — in deed, not just in words?

18.35.oldText: KING. Indeed, no place should give sanctuary to murder. Revenge should have no limits. But listen, good Laertes — here's what you should do. Stay hidden in your room. When Hamlet returns, he'll learn that you're home. We'll arrange for people to praise your skill, building on the reputation the Frenchman gave you, and bring the two of you together for a match with wagers on the outcome. He's careless, generous, and unsuspecting, so he won't inspect the swords. With a little arrangement, you can easily choose an unblunted blade and, during a practice pass, repay him for your father.

18.36.oldText: LAERTES. I'll do it. And for that purpose, I'll poison my sword. I bought a deadly ointment from a traveling salesman — so lethal that if you just dip a knife in it, no remedy on earth, no matter how rare, can save the person it scratches. I'll coat the tip of my sword with this poison, so that even the slightest scratch will kill him.

18.37.oldText: KING. Let's think this through further and consider what timing and circumstances will work best. If this plan fails and our intentions are exposed through poor execution, it would have been better not to try at all. So this scheme should have a backup — a second plan that holds if the first one doesn't work. Let me think. We'll set up a formal wager on your skills — I have it! When the fencing gets intense and you're both hot and thirsty, and he calls for a drink, I'll have a cup prepared for him — a poisoned cup. If he happens to escape your venomous blade, the cup will finish the job.

18.42.oldText: QUEEN. There's a willow that leans over a brook, showing its silver leaves reflected in the glassy stream. She went there and made wild garlands of wildflowers — crow-flowers, nettles, daisies, and long purples, which country folk give a crude name to, but modest girls call dead men's fingers. Climbing onto the overhanging branches to hang her flower wreaths, a spiteful branch snapped, and she fell, along with her weedy trophies, into the weeping brook. Her clothes spread wide and held her up like a mermaid for a while, during which time she sang snatches of old songs, as if she had no awareness of her own danger — or as if she were a creature born to that element. But it couldn't last long. Her garments, heavy with water, pulled the poor girl from her singing down to a muddy death.

19.1.oldText: FIRST CLOWN. Is she getting a Christian burial when she deliberately went and drowned herself?

19.2.oldText: SECOND CLOWN. I'm telling you she is — so dig her grave straight. The coroner held an inquest and ruled it a Christian burial.

19.5.oldText: FIRST CLOWN. It must be 'se offendendo' — it can't be anything else. Here's the point: if I drown myself on purpose, that's an act. And an act has three parts: to act, to do, and to perform. Therefore, she drowned herself on purpose.

19.7.oldText: FIRST CLOWN. Let me finish. Here's the water — good. Here's the man — good. If the man goes to the water and drowns himself, then — like it or not — he goes. Note that. But if the water comes to him and drowns him, he doesn't drown himself. Therefore, the man who isn't responsible for his own death doesn't shorten his own life.

19.11.oldText: FIRST CLOWN. Exactly right. And the real shame is that important people have more privilege in this world to drown or hang themselves than ordinary Christians do. Come, hand me my spade. There are no true gentlemen except gardeners, ditch-diggers, and grave-makers — they carry on Adam's profession.

19.19.oldText: FIRST CLOWN. I like that answer, actually — the gallows does well. But how does it do well? It does well for those who do badly. Now, you're wrong to say the gallows is stronger than the church — therefore the gallows might do well for you. Try again.

19.21.oldText: FIRST CLOWN. That's the question — figure it out.

19.24.oldText: SECOND CLOWN. Hmm — no, I can't figure it out.

19.26.oldText: FIRST CLOWN. Don't rack your brains about it anymore — beating a dull donkey won't make him go faster. And next time someone asks you that question, say 'a grave-maker.' The houses he builds last until doomsday. Now go — get yourself to the pub and fetch me some beer.

19.29.oldText: FIRST CLOWN. In youth when I was in love, in love, I thought it was very sweet. To make a deal, oh, for my advantage, oh, I thought nothing could beat it.

19.38.oldText: HAMLET. Or some courtier, who used to say, 'Good morning, sweet lord! How are you, dear lord?' This might have been Lord So-and-so, who praised Lord So-and-so's horse when he really wanted to borrow it. Isn't that possible?

19.40.oldText: HAMLET. And now it belongs to Lady Worm — jawless, and knocked around with a gravedigger's shovel. Here's a fine revolution, if only we had the insight to see it. Did it cost nothing to raise these bones, only to play bowling with them? My own bones ache to think about it.

19.44.oldText: HAMLET. There's another one. Why couldn't that be the skull of a lawyer? Where are his legal tricks now? His subtleties, his cases, his land titles, and his maneuvers? Why does he let this rude gravedigger whack him on the head with a dirty shovel without filing a lawsuit for assault? Hm!
